items.rss_description: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit? Risk Management ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:02 Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? November 19, 2026 Image On Dec. 18, Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters, and millions of us will happily pay to watch Earth's mightiest heroes face a villain bent on bringing the world to its knees. It's a great escape, partly because we know the heroes always show up in time. Real life offers no such guarantee, and last week showed how close we already live to our own doomsday script. Consider how recently the world ran on paper. Not long ago, people received a printed paycheck every week. Many of us remember our parents planning lunch hours around getting to the bank, or racing there Saturday morning before the branch closed at noon. Bills were paid by paper check, mailed to the mortgage company, the electric company and the oil company. Insuring a car or a house meant calling an agent. Buying anything "from a computer" was pure Isaac Asimov. Today, the entirety of human knowledge fits in a device the size of a deck of cards that nearly everyone carries in their pocket. That has been liberating. But it has also left us almost completely dependent on invisible systems we assume will always be on and safe from disruption, whether the threat is a malfunction, a cyberattack or simple human error. The past week showed how quickly those systems can grind to a halt. On Nov. 12, a Microsoft outage took down Outlook, Teams and Copilot – the backbone of millions of businesses – across dozens of countries for more than half a day. The next afternoon, a communications failure forced the FAA to ground every departing U.S. flight for more than four hours, the longest nationwide shutdown since 9/11. Then on Nov. 16, a software bug in JPMorgan Chase's own hardware disrupted online banking, branch transactions and Zelle payments, spilling over to customers at other banks doing business with Chase. Chase said there was no evidence the outage was cyber-related, and that is exactly the point. If an internal glitch can rattle America's biggest commercial bank, imagine what a deliberate, coordinated attack on power grids, water systems and communications networks could do. Governments urge households to keep emergency supplies, including cash, on hand. Is your company following the same advice? Do business continuity plans cover this? For many companies, the honest answer is "not really." Most plans are built for hurricanes, fires, the loss of a building and other localized events. Backups reside in another state, employees work from home, and operations shift to a recovery site. All of this assumes the Internet, the power grid, and the rest of the economy are still working somewhere . Financial regulators have pushed for more. In 2019, the FFIEC reframed its guidance from business continuity planning to business continuity management, with a focus on operational resilience and the ripple effects of outages across the financial system. The industry also created Sheltered Harbor , a standard for backing up critical customer account data nightly to an offline, air-gapped vault so customers can still reach their funds after a worst-case cyber event. Sheltered Harbor is now winding down, with its specification moving to its parent, FS-ISAC, but the principle stands. Still, even these measures assume someone, somewhere, can restore the data and run the systems. A nationwide, prolonged outage is a scenario few plans address head-on. Can companies function when the rest of the world can't? Not entirely. If customers can't reach essential services, payment rails are down and vendors go dark, no amount of preparation will preserve business as usual. But "not entirely" is materially different from "not at all." The goal is keeping your promises: knowing who your customers are, what they own and what you owe them, and honoring the most critical obligations through manual processes until systems return. That is what makes recovery possible, and it preserves trust when it matters most. Building on the plan you already have Organizations don't need to start over. They need to extend the plans they already have: Add a "dark scenario." Model a weeklong nationwide Internet and communications outage combined with an attack that corrupts your own backups. Ask what breaks first. Define minimum viable operations. For an insurer, that may mean confirming coverage, taking claims, and issuing emergency payments for catastrophic losses. For a bank, it may be cash access, balance verification, and critical payments. Everything else can wait. Keep offline, immutable copies of critical data. Maintain air-gapped backups, plus periodic printed records of policies, account balances, and key contacts. Bring back the manual playbook. Stock paper claim forms and check stock, set pre-approved emergency payment limits and clear signatory authority, and keep the procedures in print. Give a defined role to people with institutional memory of how the work got done before your digital transformation. Plan communications without the Internet. Think satellite phones, two-way radios, pre-arranged meeting points, and agreements with local broadcasters to reach customers. Pressure-test your vendors. Your plan is only as strong as your cloud providers, core processors and payment networks. Know what each would do in this scenario. Take care of your people. Employees will face the same disruption at home. Plan for staff who can't get to work, need cash, or must care for their families. Practice it. Run tabletop exercises in which nothing digital works. Gaps found in a conference room cost far less than gaps found in a crisis. Will you really be there? Nearly every bank and insurance ad promises some version of "we're there when you need us." Those promises were written with storms, fires, and floods in mind. But a slogan has no fine print. When the screens go dark, customers will expect the companies that made those promises to show up. Insurers, whose very reason for being is to anticipate the worst, are well placed to lead, both by hardening their own operations and by helping clients understand how their coverage would respond to a systemic event. Would a cyber or business interruption policy respond to a days-long cloud outage that wasn't caused by an attack? To a bank glitch that delays payroll? After last week, many risk managers are likely asking those questions for the first time. Insurers and brokers with clear answers ready will earn trust before the next outage arrives. In the end, a policy or a bank account is a promise, and trust is what customers are really buying. A company that goes silent in a crisis may never regain it. One that shows up, even with a pen, a paper form, and a phone tree, will be remembered for it. Is it really possible to be fully prepared? No organization can solve everything a large-scale shutdown would throw at it. But there is a big difference between a plan that misses a few angles and one undone by what the 9/11 Commission called a "failure of imagination." The organizations that have thought it through, protected their data, and kept manual workflows open will be the ones that help their customers first and recover fastest. In the movies, doomsday is averted by heroes in capes. In real life, it will be survived thanks to the continuity planner with a binder of printed procedures, the claims veteran who remembers how to cut a paper check, and the IT lead who already knows which vendor to call. They are the real superheroes. Now is the time to give them what they need. Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? Diane Brassard James Ballot

items.title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.original_title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.rss_title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.rss_description: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline Talent Gap ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:05 As AI automates entry-level insurance tasks, insurance industry leaders must design experiences to develop professional judgment in emerging talent. November 19, 2026 Image Back in the '90s, I was a beast at reconciling spreadsheets. The 10 fingers I'm using to type these lines used to set my "10-key" numeric keypad ablaze. But if you're among the younger readers to come across this article, you'll have no idea what I'm talking about. And as a society, I think that's for the best. A core promise of technological advancement is to eliminate drudgery, like using a 10-key to enter vast amounts of numeric data. In property and casualty insurance, we have spent decades trying to remove mundane work from the lives of underwriters, claims professionals, and technologists. We made great strides with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), leaps with broader Intelligent Automation (IA), and now a phenomenal bound with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises to revolutionize the way we work. But amid the terrific change lurks an industry-scale problem. While our job definitions and related skills are morphing at an absurdly fast rate, how do we ensure that emerging talent has the opportunity to develop the depth of understanding and judgment their predecessors possess, even while AI is tending to disassociate humans from some of the traditional activities of their craft? That replacement system needs a name and, more importantly, an owner. Architecting Experience is the framework of deliberately designed exposures, decisions, and feedback loops through which people develop professional judgment and decision context. Cracks in the career ladder Stanford's Digital Economy Lab analyzed payroll data on millions of U.S. jobs through June 2026 and found no economy-wide displacement from AI. What they did find was new employment among 22- to 25-year-olds lagging in industries heavily affected by AI, by about 19% compared to less-affected industries.[1] The employment ladder isn't broken, but some rungs at the bottom are disappearing, which makes it a whole lot harder to climb. Even where junior positions aren't disappearing, the formative skills they help develop are the easiest to automate. In insurance, applied experience and apprenticeship have built the tacit knowledge and judgment needed for success for generations. After ingesting enough submissions, you develop a second sense for when a detail looks off, or when risks that look identical stem from entirely different causes. But when this repetitive and seemingly menial work is delegated to AI, younger staff are deprived of the very task-level experiences they need to develop the business EQ, empathy, and scar tissue that will someday make them senior. What our young talent are left with are the tasks too difficult for AI, and sometimes beyond the judgment they possess. In their 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, PwC looked at over a billion job advertisements. They found that heavily AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand senior capabilities—like judgment, leadership, and interpersonal skills—than the jobs least exposed to AI. PwC described the trend as the "seniorization" of junior work.[2] A short-term view of AI-driven task optimization will only make the problem worse. For senior employees, more demanding tasks feel more meaningful and engaging than rote work. But the type of work that is most interesting to a seasoned professional isn't necessarily the type of work best suited to creating one. And meaningful work sounds wonderful until every task is a demanding one, and the much-needed Easy Tuesday becomes as much of a relic as my most trusty 10-digit keypad. Clear the slop from the stream BCG recently surveyed 11,749 workers across 14 markets about their use of AI at work. Two-thirds of regular AI users reported increased job satisfaction. At the same time, 41% reported increased mental strain. Half said they were spending more time managing and directing AI than doing the underlying work itself.[3] "Brain fry" refers to the mental fatigue associated with information overload from increased AI oversight.[4] With AI, any junior underwriter can generate a 40-page report with the aplomb of a managing director. But then, the report has to be checked. Preferably by someone with enough know-how to identify and correct mistakes. Without guardrails, we quickly end up in a system where our young talent can access AI-powered tools that allow them to produce work that looks good, but is actually riddled with problems. These problems are then sent upstream to more senior resources who have to spend their time fixing this "workslop"[5]. Junior professionals learn nothing in the process, and increase the workload of their most knowledgeable, and often most expensive, colleagues. When we claim AI is changing the way we work, we're giving the tool too much credit, while absolving ourselves of responsibility. The truth is, AI isn't changing the way we work. Our decision-makers are. And if, as a result of these changes and the adoption of AI, the leaders break the career ladder, they are responsible for engineering a new one. AI-resilient architecture I'm not in favor of clinging to rote work out of nostalgia. AI very much has a place in our workflows, and I remain bullish on the beneficial role of AI over the long term. But today, as we are all still sorting out the impacts and influences of AI on real people, we must think things through holistically and humanistically from the very beginning. In the face of AI removing traditional and lower-level tasks, the implications of this must be assessed, and solutions for the resultant gaps must be created. When architecting experience for new talent, what matters is to look at tasks through the dual lens of raw efficiency and professional development. Do the tasks teach the rules of the game, and more importantly, when the rules stop applying? Do they offer a chance to shadow a more seasoned professional to develop situational awareness and understanding of context? Do they help build judgment? Do they create the kinds of relationships every business is built on? These answers will help inform which tasks to automate, and which need more thought. A "yes" doesn't mean the task cannot be handed off to automation; it means the developmental value has to be preserved, somehow. The oversight role for management is to understand and enforce the right order of operations: organic brain first, neural network second. As with all complex systems, architecting experience isn't a blueprint. It's a process bound to yield different results for different organizations. Once the initial assessment is complete, ideally under the supervision of an executive with accountability, the hard work of execution, review, and adaptation begins. The good news is: there's plenty of responsibility to go around. Executive management must identify the experiences that create expertise, design a plan for succession, and own how the business will look ten years down the road. Elsewhere, HR and development teams have a responsibility to engineer the learning experiences and coaching or apprenticeship infrastructure, while managers can iterate, suggest improvements, and raise the red flag when skills aren't being developed. Tech and risk teams also have a clear role to observe AI usage, monitor costs and defect rates, and flag when automated work misses the mark. Senior professionals must keep in mind that juniors need engagement, context, and good professional models to follow, while the juniors themselves must remember to think first and ask AI second. Insurance is still early in the AI adoption process, and fortunate to have a deep bench of experienced professionals around the world, alongside ambitious newcomers. But every day, AI offers new deployment opportunities for efficiency and optimization. The greatest organizations of tomorrow will not only be able to harness those opportunities, but will also succeed in architecting experience for the next generation of world-class talent. Bob Pick November 19, 2026 Back in the '90s, I was a beast at reconciling spreadsheets. The 10 fingers I'm using to type these lines used to set my "10-key" numeric keypad ablaze. But if you're among the younger readers to come across this article, you'll have no idea what I'm talking about. And as a society, I think that's for the best. A core promise of technological advancement is to eliminate drudgery, like using a 10-key to enter vast amounts of numeric data. In property and casualty insurance, we have spent decades trying to remove mundane work from the lives of underwriters, claims professionals, and technologists. We made great strides with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), leaps with broader Intelligent Automation (IA), and now a phenomenal bound with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises to revolutionize the way we work. But amid the terrific change lurks an industry-scale problem. While our job definitions and related skills are morphing at an absurdly fast rate, how do we ensure that emerging talent has the opportunity to develop the depth of understanding and judgment their predecessors possess, even while AI is tending to disassociate humans from some of the traditional activities of their craft? Even where junior positions aren't disappearing, the formative skills they help develop are the easiest to automate. In insurance, applied experience and apprenticeship have built the tacit knowledge and judgment needed for success for generations. After ingesting enough submissions, you develop a second sense for when a detail looks off, or when risks that look identical stem from entirely different causes. What our young talent are left with are the tasks too difficult for AI, and sometimes beyond the judgment they possess. They found that heavily AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand senior capabilities—like judgment, leadership, and interpersonal skills—than the jobs least exposed to AI. PwC described the trend as the "seniorization" of junior work.[2] A short-term view of AI-driven task optimization will only make the problem worse. For senior employees, more demanding tasks feel more meaningful and engaging than rote work. But the type of work that is most interesting to a seasoned professional isn't necessarily the type of work best suited to creating one. items.title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.original_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_description: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:15 Four-year producer retention has sat near 14% for years. One overlooked cause: new producers are handed materials that promote the company but give prospects no reason to trust the person. November 19, 2026 Image Even with aptitude and personality testing, only about 14% of new financial professionals have still been under contract four years after they were hired, according to LIMRA. The losses come early. First-year retention runs from 44% to 55%, depending on who recruited the producer. When a new producer leaves within two years, the recruiting effort, the licensing, the training, and the manager's time are lost. The industry has refined selection, adjusted financing plans, and built mentoring programs. Yet the four-year number has barely moved. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. I've come to believe we're overlooking one piece of the problem: the gap between marketing and sales. Marketing departments produce great materials that promote the brand and its products. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. Conventional e-newsletters contribute to inbox glut Most new producers are sent out with the same tools as everyone else: a business card, perhaps a company newsletter, and a set of pre-approved PDFs. The newsletter is the piece most firms count on to keep prospects warm, and it has five weaknesses. They are too long. Attention spans are short, and screen after screen asks for more time than most readers will give. They make readers scroll to choose. Readers scroll down to see what's there, then back up to decide. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. They lack creative calls to action or lead magnets of value. Readers see a "Subscribe" or "Get my 5 tips" button as permission to receive spam. They speak for the company, not the person. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. A better newsletter respects the reader's time: one page with links to no more than three pieces of content. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. What a first impression could be Social media posts, newsletters, mail, and product information all have their place in the sales cycle, but on their own, none of them builds a relationship. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. In large organizations, lead gates usually sit on the company website, not on individual producers' pages, so the contact information goes to the company or agency. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. Put together, these elements give a new producer something memorable that builds trust: a personal profile, an approved multimedia brochure, and a way to find the people worth calling. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. It requires looking at a new producer's first 90 days from the prospect's side of the table. Audit the first impression. Gather everything a new producer can send a prospect in week one. Then ask: Why would I choose this producer over another? Put the person up front. Give each new producer a short video or audio introduction about who they are, not what they do. All your producers do similar work. Who they are is what sets them apart. Cover every format. Pair each key message with something to read, something to watch or hear, and something to try. In a newsletter, that means no more than three pieces, each labeled with its format and length. Host it; don't attach it. Sharing content by link keeps the company in control and ensures only approved, up-to-date materials circulate. Watch the early signals. Lack of activity is an early warning sign, and analytics can now measure it. Managers can see which channels drive activity and which new recruits may need help sooner. Have it ready before the first appointment. A fast start depends on what the producer can share in the first week, not the first quarter. Give them something worth answering Pushing prospects with a stick instead of offering a carrot gives the industry a black eye. The better path is to make sure that when prospects look, they find a real person, in a format they can take in, with content that compliance approved and still under control. The four-year retention number has held steady for a long time. Leaders have told us that early activity matters. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. items.title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.original_title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.rss_title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.rss_description: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps Cyber ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/18/2026 - 14:34 The $6.3 billion Binance theft bypassed private keys entirely, exposing gaps in how crypto risks are underwritten and covered. November 19, 2026 Image On Oct. 29, attackers took roughly $6.3 billion out of Binance's hot wallets in about 20 minutes. It is the largest crypto theft on record, and the FBI has tied it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance has since committed to absorbing the financial impact of the incident. By Oct. 31, it reported that 98% of the affected token assets had been replenished. How it happened matters more than how much According to Binance's incident report, the campaign ran for months. One engineer installed a tampered developer tool in June. Another was compromised in September through a fake coding assignment. In October, the attackers used an internal AI tool to get into more machines and finally took control of the system that approves wallet transactions. The key detail for insurance: Binance says no private keys were stolen. The attackers didn't need them. They controlled the system that signs transactions, so it signed whatever the attackers asked. Underwriting conversations with crypto clients have long centered on keys. Where are they stored? Who holds them? How many people have to sign off? This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. What brokers should review before the next renewal Map the gaps. Lay the crime, specie, cyber, tech E&O, and D&O policies side by side and walk through this scenario. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Ben Slagis

Underwriting conversations with crypto clients have long centered on keys. Where are they stored? Who holds them? How many people have to sign off? This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. items.rss_description: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech PaulCarroll Mon, 11/16/2026 - 17:10 When I ran the editing operation for the Wall Street Journal's European edition in the '80s, the "lockup" at midnight (or so) was frequently so chaotic that I posited what I called Carroll's law. Building on Murphy's law – everything that can go wrong will go wrong – Carroll's law said Murphy was an optimist. I'm feeling déjà vu , given all the technology-related chaos of the past week, centered on Friday the 13th, when all U.S. air traffic was shut down for hours and Microsoft's Outlook was only intermittently operating after a full-on outage the day before, for what amounts to the email backbone for the world economy. As much as there are individual reasons for those outages and other recent ones, the problems point to a pattern. The transition we're going through to a completely wired, AI world is so fundamental that two things are true: 1) We need to be a lot more careful about work like the upgrades to the FAA system, and we can head off a lot of problems if we are. 2) There will still be chaos from time to time, including for the insurance industry, especially as we start to roll out AI agents. So buckle up. Let's have a look. I first started thinking a couple of weeks ago about writing about the risks that arise from connecting everything to everything through the Internet of Things. The impetus was a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems throughout Europe – including in France, the U.K., Italy, Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg and Estonia – followed by similar attacks on commissaries at U.S. military installations. The hackers raised the temperature inside 900 freezer units across 17 countries to as high as 120 degrees Fahrenheit, causing millions of dollars of food to go bad overnight and be thrown out. France, which suffered two-thirds of the attacks on freezers, blamed Iran, and geopolitical tensions could well lead to such attacks. North Korea, Russia and China all have active military cyber units. It's also possible that teenagers who in the past might have spraypainted graffiti on a school wall will now use AI to indulge their anger and show off in much more destructive ways. In any case, the cyber attacks show that the power of the IoT comes with a potential downside. Connecting essentially every device to every other device gives hackers more routes into systems they want to attack. And industrial systems, such as those that let supermarkets monitor and manage refrigeration centrally typically aren't built to the same security specifications that the main IT systems are. Insurers will have to be alert both about clients and about themselves. Clients may suffer theft, business interruption, claims of negligence against directors and officers, and so on. Insurers may face attacks themselves as they link to more sensors, third-party data sources, and providers of digital services such as payments. Insurers certainly make juicy targets, given all the important information they have on individuals and businesses. The Wall Street Journal published a story with the headline, " Supermarket-Fridge Hacks Show Risk of Linking Everything to the Internet" , that said: "Artificial intelligence suddenly makes the problem much bigger, because hackers are automating their hunt for exposed web connections and running searches at blistering speeds." The article adds that 20% of IoT devices already have at least one known cybersecurity vulnerability. It turns out, though, that the refrigerator cyberattacks were just the start. On Thursday, bleeding into Friday, Microsoft's Outlook email system went down. As Wired wrote in a story headlined " The Microsoft Outage Is a Warning for the World ": " The outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge." Full details on the cause of the outage have yet to be provided. At the least, it shows the danger of concentration for a key service such as communication. We've actually seen even more, though smaller, examples of dangerous concentration just since Friday. United Airlines, which controls a major chunk of air travel in the U.S. and internationally, had to delay all departing flights for more than an hour and a half on Monday because of a software issue. A technical glitch with software at Chase Bank delayed online banking and caused transaction glitches for both itself and other major banks. Concentration will only increase from here, so we need to be prepared for the fact that a single problem can cause widespread trouble. There is some speculation that AI may have played a role in the Outlook trouble, given that Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees in July and just offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 people, or 27% of its workforce, while saying the company is turning more coding work over to AI. Which brings us to the FAA communications disaster that shut down air travel for five hours in the U.S. on Friday. The current official explanation is that a single, old router in Arkansas was overwhelmed during an upgrade to new technology, but some officials initially said an upgrade to AI technology known as SMART may also have been involved. Oddly, the disagreement is very public and at the cabinet level – the secretary of Transportation insists the AI work had no bearing on the outage, while the secretary of Homeland Security has suggested at least twice that the AI initiative may have been to blame. Whatever the exact problem, the FAA issue should be the simplest to avoid. It just requires some basic hygiene. For instance, you have to give yourself a way to instantly undo an upgrade if it starts to go south. And whatever you do, you don't do a major upgrade during a busy period -- such as a Friday afternoon, when millions of people are flying somewhere for the weekend. You do the upgrade in the middle of the night, when a problem can be corrected before much of anyone notices. But people will ignore basic principles of software management, just as they'll be too reliant on single sources of key digital services such as communication and will be too slow to tackle the vulnerabilities that come from connecting to systems and services that aren't secure enough. And AI will greatly accelerate the pace at which problems surface. So we should consider recent events as warnings of future problems, not as one-offs. There is good news in the short term, though, for those of you who are superstitious types. Friday wasn't just the 13th; an astrology-curious acquaintance tells me Mercury and Venus both ended their retrogrades that day, bringing some supposed relief after weeks of celestial troublemaking. (Mercury, I'm told, can be especially problematic. It's blamed for everything from miscommunications to travel mishaps.) But both planets have resumed their normal forward movement across the sky, so astrologers give us an all clear – or at least a mostly clear, because the planets' "shadow" periods will last for a few weeks. Cheers,' Paul P.S. I later learned, courtesy of Google, that many people had beaten me to the Carroll adaptation of Murphy's law. Oh, well. P.P.S. My favorite tweet on the tech outages: "If you booked your United Airlines flight through your Chase Bank account and need to access those records on your Outlook, what do you do?" Image Paul Carroll The air traffic debacle and email outage on Friday don't just call for more careful management of our technology. They also offer a stark warning. Friday wasn't just the 13th; an astrology-curious acquaintance tells me Mercury and Venus both ended their retrogrades that day, bringing some supposed relief after weeks of celestial troublemaking. (Mercury, I'm told, can be especially problematic. It's blamed for everything from miscommunications to travel mishaps.) But both planets have resumed their normal forward movement across the sky, so astrologers give us an all clear – or at least a mostly clear, because the planets' "shadow" periods will last for a few weeks. Cheers,' Paul P.S. I later learned, courtesy of Google, that many people had beaten me to the Carroll adaptation of Murphy's law. Oh, well. P.P.S. My favorite tweet on the tech outages: "If you booked your United Airlines flight through your Chase Bank account and need to access those records on your Outlook, what do you do?" items.extracted_text: ILS and alternative capital expanding footprint into DUAE market: AM Best - Artemis.bm ILS and alternative capital expanding footprint into DUAE market: AM Best 23rd November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard In a new commentary, rating agency AM Best has highlighted how alternative capital and insurance-linked securities (ILS) are increasingly entering the delegated underwriting authority enterprise (DUAE) space, with DUAEs utilising sidecars, catastrophe bonds, and collateralized reinsurance to secure capacity when insurers step back. In its latest market segment outlook, AM Best has maintained its stable outlook for the DUAE segment, with the agency citing an anticipated moderation in premium growth amid more disciplined expansion efforts. The agency explained that the DUAE market managed to post its fifth consecutive year of double-digit premium growth, outpacing the broader U.S. property and casualty industry. However, analysts cautioned that momentum is expected to wind down as regulators and capacity providers place greater emphasis on long term underwriting quality, transparency, and loss ratio stability rather than short term premium growth. Further into the report, AM Best said delegated underwriting businesses are important strategic partners for capacity providers, particularly in emerging risks, specialty lines, and technology-based platforms. The competitive landscape is also intensifying as insurers face competition from alternative capital and ILS increasingly entering the space, often seeking diversified noncorrelated risk through quota share treaties or fronting arrangements. “The result is a blended capacity environment where capacity provider balance sheets provide support while other alternative capital sources add flexibility, speed, and appetite for emerging or specialty risk. Private equity capital, for example, continues to flow into the segment, driving mergers and acquisitions, where smaller and less-differentiated players are likely to become acquisition targets,” AM Best said. The agency continued: “While overall capacity remains available, it is increasingly partner specific, with capacity providers distinguishing sharply between DUAEs that deliver predictable, disciplined results and those with more volatile performance. This reflects a shift toward profitability, governance, and long-term alignment rather than pure growth.” AM Best further emphasised that delegated underwriting authority enterprises are also using ILS structures to secure further backing. “Fronting carriers bridge capacity gaps by ceding underlying risk to fully collateralized ILS structures that may be funded by third-party capital. DUAEs are increasingly utilizing sidecars, catastrophe bonds, and collateralized reinsurance to secure backing if traditional insurers are not willing. At the same time, there is consolidation within specialty distribution channels, driven by firms seeking scale, technology capabilities, and a broader market reach,” the agency explains. Jacqalene Lentz, senior director, AM Best, said: “The regulatory environment is moving toward stronger governance practices, as well as deeper scrutiny of DUAEs as the segment has faced criticism in the past. items.rss_title: Nvidia Reinstates Huang as CEO, Trump Says No Risk to Security

items.extracted_text: Nvidia Reinstates Huang as CEO, Trump Says No Risk to Security Article 5 Comments Nvidia Corp.’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer less than two weeks following his remarkable ouster, after US government support. Nvidia shares gained more than 31%. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, board chair, in a company statement Monday. Huang’s return is effective immediately, according to the statement. The board reinstated Huang after a series of meetings and discussions and after receiving input from “senior levels of the United States government,” according to the company. “Based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Huang, 63, oversaw Nvidia for more than three decades and built it into the world’s biggest chipmaker. The company officially parted ways with Huang on Nov. 12, after revelations about his extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom the US reportedly believes was spying on behalf of China, turned into a widening scandal. The Department of Justice is investigating the woman, Alice Huang, and her company Megaspeed for potential artificial intelligence chip smuggling. Beijing has denied the espionage plot. Huang had publicly appealed to the company’s board about reinstating him, a move that was supported by some employees and prominent Silicon Valley figures. Still, the had board rejected that overture earlier this week. President Donald Trump — who has built a close relationship with Huang since his term began — has voiced support for the chief executive since the news broke that the US was investigating his relationship with the suspected spy. Trump had repeatedly defended the ousted CEO, praising his abilities, saying Huang had learned a big lesson and noting that he would not mind if Huang returned. Over the weekend, the president intensified that support by saying that he hoped Nvidia’s board would rehire Huang. The president hailed the CEO’s return in a Truth Social post on Monday, saying the board had made “the correct and proper decision.” Trump said that the US government doesn’t believe that Huang’s return to Nvidia would pose “any risk” to national security, adding that authorities didn’t have any evidence that the chip magnate had engaged in any unlawful conduct. Nvidia’s board has formed a committee of independent directors to investigate reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the company said. The investigation will proceed to its conclusion, the company said. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said in the statement. Nvidia is the top maker of artificial intelligence accelerators — the chips that train and run AI models — making it the biggest beneficiary of runaway spending on data center infrastructure. Late last year, following lobbying from Huang, Trump decided to loosen chip controls and allow Nvidia to sell its H200 processor, now generations behind its latest Vera Rubin chips, to China. Colette Kress, who briefly served as interim CEO told investors last week that the company would stop selling even licensed H200 products to China. items.extracted_text: Wisconsin Regulator Urges Prompt Claims Settlement Processes From July Storms Article 0 Comments The Wisconsin Office of the Insurance Commissioner (OCI) issued a bulletin on Nov. 20 reminding insurers that the office expects a timely claims settlement process for property damage losses resulting from the late July storms that hit the state. On July 26, northeast Wisconsin experienced extreme storms, tornado and hail, causing many residents to be displaced from their homes. Many homes have been deemed unsafe or inaccessible by local officials, according to the OCI. The bulletin sent out last week urges insurers to promptly respond to pertinent communications from consumers and complete their claims investigation with “all reasonable dispatch.” Failure to adequately respond to claims may constitute an unfair method and practice in the business of insurance under Wisconsin law, the bulletin said. The full bulletin can be found here . items.extracted_text: CalPERS highlights growing ILS investments as a use-case in diversification - Artemis.bm CalPERS highlights growing ILS investments as a use-case in diversification 23rd November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The California Public Employees’ Retirement System, or CalPERS, sees its entry into the insurance-linked securities investment market as a use-case in diversification and following its success, the giant pension investor is establishing a program to incubate diversifying strategies of this kind. Most recently, on CalPERS activities in investing into insurance-linked securities and third-party reinsurance strategy funds, we reported in September that the combined valuation of its allocations to the ILS asset class neared $2.5 billion at the mid-point of 2026 , an increase of around 70% just in the first-half of this year. Since then, we also highlighted a report that CalPERS has been exploring ways to increase its exposure to insurance-linked securities , which are seen as one asset class that can contribute towards its goal to invest $100 billion in climate solutions by 2030. Now, we’ve learned from the pension’s latest disclosures that in the quarter to June 30th 2026, CalPERS increased its allocation allowance for so-called “ILS Opportunistic Strategies” to $850 million. That likely flowed in with the increase we saw at the mid-year valuation, but there is also a chance some of it remained un-deployed, or is planned for year-end. Given how quickly the pension investor ramped up there is a chance this continues with more added to its ILS investment holdings for 2027, potentially with an additional access point of some description as CalPERS clearly wants to diversify across managers within the ILS asset class as well. It now transpires that allocating to insurance-linked securities has provided a well-timed use-case in diversification for CalPERS, as it continues to shift its investment strategy to better suit the recently adopted total portfolio approach. As of July 1st 2026, CalPERS adopted the total portfolio approach, replacing the previously utilised strategic asset allocation model that guided its investment decision-making. Diversification is a key component of the total portfolio approach, in particular in being able to identify the source of alpha within asset classes, as well as its correlation. CalPERS is building this out through analysis of different investment strategies and interestingly the investment committee sees the work undertaken to enter and allocate to the ILS asset class as a foundation it can now build-on. In a similar way to how it has embraced ILS, CalPERS intends to incubate a so-called diversifying multi-strategy initiative, which is presumably a way to establish an allocation in a new asset class, better understand its sources of alpha, return profile, liquidity etc, before bringing it into the total portfolio. ILS is, of course, among the most diversifying and least correlated asset classes around, so the learnings CalPERS’ investment team will have gleaned from ramping up and diversifying across specialist managers within the ILS asset class, will be educational in how the pension investor can approach other diversifying assets over time. It also shows that CalPERS entry into ILS has been well thought-through and planned, resulting in a kind of framework for diversifying assets it can use to help it optimise its sources of alpha and return. Given global uncertainty and recent events around the world, CalPERS investment teams recognise the value diversification can bring and even see a more diversified approach, with lower expected one-year returns, as potentially less volatile over-time, with better long-term return outcomes deemed possible. This is precisely the kind of strategic approach to diversification that ILS fits into so well and can add meaningful value to, for large investors like CalPERS. It also underscores that CalPERS sees the ILS investments as a strategic allocation, while the increased commitment allowances we’ve seen and the comments around how it can help them allocate more to climate solutions, all point to ILS being an asset class CalPERS will likely increase over-time. In order for an asset class like ILS to be meaningful to an investor the size of CalPERS it also needs a certain level of scale. So it will be interesting to see how the investor manages the current softening reinsurance and catastrophe bond market environment, as well as when or if it looks to upsize in the asset class again. The California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS) is just one of the numerous pension fund and major ILS investors we track in our directories here . items.extracted_text: Atrium and CRC launch Fractal Re II third-party capital backed reinsurance portfolio at Lloyd's - Artemis.bm Atrium and CRC launch Fractal Re II third-party capital backed reinsurance portfolio at Lloyd’s 23rd November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Atrium, a Lloyd’s underwriter that is part of the CRC Group, is set to benefit from third-party capital investor backed reinsurance capacity to support program business from its parent through a new Fractal Re II portfolio deal, arranged with the help of the CRC Risk Solutions division. Fractal Re II features a diversified reinsurance portfolio of property, specialty and casualty risks that will be underwritten via Atrium’s Syndicate 2026. The firm’s announced today, that Fractal Re II succeeds the Fractal Re I transaction, and will deliver capacity to the Lloyd’s market from a collective of sophisticated third-party capital providers. CRC Group is a pure-play specialty wholesale, managing general agency and program management business based in North America. Atrium became part of CRC Group in 2025, but continues to underwrite independently. Bill Goldstein, Vice Chair and Head of Strategic Partnerships, Capacity and Capital Solutions at CRC, explained, “The launch of Fractal Re II reflects our commitment to developing market-leading solutions that strengthen connectivity between insurers, reinsurers and capital, to deliver better outcomes across the insurance ecosystem.” John Fowle, CEO, Atrium, added, “Atrium are delighted to deliver a compelling demonstration of both the strength of the Lloyd’s model and the benefits of our membership of CRC Group to our capital providers.” Rachel Grunert, Active Underwriter, Syndicate 2026, further stated, “The development of the Fractal Re II solution represents a key milestone for Atrium as the first Portfolio underwriting acceptance into Syndicate 2026. “We are excited to be developing our model in line with our plans and ahead of schedule.” For Atrium, this is an effective way to access third-party capital providers to support its reinsurance of a CRC underwriting portfolio, it seems. While for CRC, it enables the firm to utilise its recently acquired at the start of this year, Lloyd’s platform access via Atrium to mobilise efficient reinsurance capacity. A Fractal Re transaction involving CRC was previously known to be a quota share sidecar structure, under Bermuda vehicle Fractal Re Ltd . That arrangement in 2024 saw $270 million of collateralized reinsurance capacity for certain casualty risk focused programs secured written by CRC’s Starwind Specialty Insurance Services, LLC. This Fractal Re II arrangements appears to be the succession and evolution of that transaction, perhaps also an expansion to include other lines of business, given the first was a casualty ILS deal and this one includes property, specialty and casualty lines from CRC programs. Now Fractal Re II channels a broader set of risks from CRC Underwriting, with reinsurance provided via Atrium in the Lloyd’s marketplace, while still being backed by third-party capital providers. It’s not immediately clear what the underlying risk transfer structures are in this case, or whether the Lloyd’s insurance-linked securities (ILS) structure London Bridge 2 PCC may have been utilised. We have reached out to Atrium for comment and will update this article if any further details are made available. items.extracted_text: Former Iowa Insurance Agency Owner Sentenced for Wire Fraud Article 0 Comments The former owner of an Iowa insurance agency was sentenced to prison last week for creating and falsely submitting insurance claims under policyholders’ accounts. April Johnson, 46, of Montrose, Iowa, was sentenced on Nov. 17 to three years in federal prison for two counts of wire fraud. Johnson listed herself or a family member as the payee for the false claims, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Southern District of Iowa. Johnson obtained payments issued as a result of the false claims. She engaged in the scheme from approximately 2016 to 2023, causing over $550,000 in loss. Johnson was ordered to pay $758,000 in restitution and will be required to serve three years of supervised release following her imprisonment. Topics Fraud Was this article valuable? items.rss_title: Historic Winner of Texas Oil Regulator Seat Wants Faster Permits

items.extracted_text: Historic Winner of Texas Oil Regulator Seat Wants Faster Permits Article 0 Comments The first Democrat in 36 years to win a seat on the commission that governs the oil and gas industry in Texas said he plans to work with his Republican colleagues to speed up permitting in the state. Texas Railroad Commission member-elect Jon Rosenthal said he aims to find ways to incentivize the industry to expand “responsibly” and did not express plans to reduce oil production in the state. “We should be partnering with folks in the industry because they’re the ones who understand this intimately,” Rosenthal said Friday in an interview with Bloomberg. “I’ve talked to folks out there in the real world who have been working on this permit or that permit for months or even years. They’re way behind.” The three-member commission is responsible for overseeing the $200 billion Texas oil and gas industry. Its purview expanded from managing freight rates more than 100 years ago to handling drilling permits and well inspections as well as enforcing safety and pollution rules. The agency provided the template for OPEC’s founders in 1960. Rosenthal defeated Republican firebrand Bo French on Nov. 3 amid a so-called blue wave that saw Texas Democrats sweep the governor’s office, a US senate seat and a host of down-ballot races in the state. A self-described “drill-baby-drill Democrat,” Rosenthal is no stranger to the energy industry. He worked for 25 years as a mechanical engineer for some of the world’s biggest oil field contractors, including SLB and NOV Inc. Rosenthal is also familiar with the state legislature as he’s wrapping up a fourth term as a state representative from the Houston area. One of his main priorities is beefing up the commission’s ranks. “I am going to strongly advocate for increased funding, not just for ramping up well plugging, which clearly needs to happen, but also to hire some more folks at the agency to raise their pay scale so that we can be more competitive,” said Rosenthal, who served on the legislature’s Energy Resources Committee, which oversees the Railroad Commission. “There’s some new leadership that my existing relationships I think will be helpful to our effort as a commission.” Since the US midterms, Rosenthal said he’s met with Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick as well as outgoing Commissioner Jim Wright, a Republican who lost to French in the primary. Rosenthal said he plans to meet with the other sitting commissioner, Wayne Christian, in about a week. “We do our best work in the legislature and in these agencies when we seek common ground with our colleagues from across the political spectrum,” said Rosenthal. “I just literally cannot wait to get into this role.” Photo: Jon Rosenthal, a Democrat from Texas, returns to the House Chamber during a special session at the Texas State Capitol in Austin, Texas, US, on Monday, Aug. 18, 2025. items.rss_title: YouTube Finalizing Multibillion-Dollar Settlement With Schools Over Social Media Addiction Claims
items.rss_description: Google’s YouTube is finalizing a multibillion-dollar settlement payout to school districts across the U.S. that have accused the company of designing an addictive video platform that has damaged the mental health of students, people familiar with the matter said. YouTube …
items.extracted_text: YouTube Finalizing Multibillion-Dollar Settlement With Schools Over Social Media Addiction Claims Article 0 Comments Google’s YouTube is finalizing a multibillion-dollar settlement payout to school districts across the U.S. that have accused the company of designing an addictive video platform that has damaged the mental health of students, people familiar with the matter said. YouTube has reached an agreement in principle to potentially pay around $3 billion to thousands of school districts, say the people, who asked not to be identified discussing confidential information. That would make it the largest corporate settlement ever reached with school districts in the U.S. The deal with YouTube includes additional product safeguards for teens. Google spokesman José Castaneda declined to comment on the settlement, as did the plaintiffs attorneys co-leading the school district cases in federal court. If finalized, the settlement would allow YouTube to avoid a major wave of litigation with the schools — a crucial arena for its business model. YouTube is deeply embedded in the lives of students, both outside and inside U.S. classrooms, where Google’s Chromebook is the most commonly used student laptop. Many teachers say they use YouTube for instructional purposes, making schools a particularly consequential legal battleground for the company. As the settlement over addiction claims is finalized, Google has faced a separate backlash with schools over its refusal to block AI chatbot features from search tools used by students. On Thursday, hundreds of Google employees urged their employer to allow schools to use Google Search without AI chatbots and the controversy is ongoing. The deal, which is contingent on a majority of the school districts signing on, will likely take a few months to officially finalize. This litigation marks one of the few times that the districts have exercised their collective action against a corporation in a mass tort, where multiple lawsuits are bundled together to streamline the pretrial process but each case is handled independently. YouTube’s historic deal with schools comes amid a global backlash against social media, with growing concerns that the companies profit at the expense of their teen users’ mental health. More than 10,000 lawsuits have been filed against YouTube, Meta Platforms Inc., Snap Inc. and TikTok Inc. in the past five years by schools, individuals and state attorneys general, accusing them of creating products as addictive as cigarettes and targeting them to minors, just like Big Tobacco. The lawsuits claim that the platforms’ features, including limitless scrolling and autoplay video, have warped a generation of children, causing addiction, depression, anxiety, eating disorders and suicide. In August, Meta reached a landmark deal involving almost every US state in which the company agreed to pay as much as $18 billion and to make sweeping product changes, including a two-hour daily limit on teen scrolling. While individual plaintiffs are seeking compensation for personal losses, the school districts want reimbursement for the institutional costs of social media addiction – including burgeoning mental health and counseling services for students. The districts have argued that the companies knew about the mental health risks for youth, but failed to design features to reduce the addictive nature of the products. (Thousands of the individual personal-injury lawsuits against YouTube remain active.) The first bellwether social-media addiction trial involving a claim by a school was scheduled to begin in June, but all four defendants settled with the rural Kentucky school district a month before. The companies paid a combined $27 million to avoid trial with the Breathitt County School District, which is nestled in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains and has fewer than 2,000 students. In that earlier settlement, YouTube negotiated a payout of slightly more than $2 million and was the only company that also agreed to provide the district with training programs, according to documents released under Kentucky’s open records law. Meta paid $9 million while Snap and TikTok each paid $8 million. In written statements, the companies said they had resolved the case amicably and would continue to invest in stronger safeguards for their users. The next federal case centers on a school district in Tucson, Arizona, with about 40,000 students. The trial is scheduled to begin in February before a judge in Oakland, California, who is overseeing all the school district cases. Three defendants remain: Meta, TikTok and Snap.
